title: Prayer - Part 6: How We Are to Pray
speaker: Mr. Alex Lyro
summary: This lesson explores Westminster Larger Catechism questions 185 and 186, detailing the attitudes and dispositions required for true prayer. The speaker breaks down fifteen distinct characteristics of proper prayer including reverence, humility, sincerity, faith, fervency, love, and perseverance, then introduces the Lord's Prayer as the special rule directing our prayer life.

outline.title: The Heart Orientation Required in Prayer (Question 185)
subpoints: Awful apprehension of God's majesty - reverential realization of God's infinite greatness and separation from creation
Deep sense of our unworthiness - humility recognizing we are dust and ashes with no claims on God
Consciousness of our necessities - honest awareness of physical and spiritual needs
Confession of sin - acknowledgment of sinfulness, not mere external penance
Penitent heart - hating sin and turning from it, not just confessing it
Thankful heart - specific, sustained recognition of God's blessings beyond mere courtesy
Enlarged heart - pouring out one's soul with fervent desire for God's answer and communion

outline.title: The Intellectual and Spiritual Qualities of Prayer
subpoints: Understanding - praying with the mind and insight into God's revelation; knowledge of Scripture
Faith - essential trust in God's character, promises, and redemptive work
Sincerity - no pretense or performance; bringing one's real heart to God
Fervency - earnestness and warmth of heart, not emotional display or dramatic performance

outline.title: The Relational and Persevering Dimensions of Prayer
subpoints: Love - guarding against empty duty; praying for others out of genuine love
Perseverance - continuing to pray even when answers are delayed or not apparent
Waiting upon the Lord - active trust and remaining steadfast in God's promises
Humble submission to God's will - yielding our desires to God's authority

outline.title: The Rule Governing Prayer (Question 186)
subpoints: The whole word of God directs our prayer - Scripture commands, promises, models, and establishes boundaries for prayer
The Lord's Prayer as the special rule - the only prayer Jesus explicitly taught his disciples
The Lord's Prayer as a pattern and measure - it summarizes biblical prayer categories and guards against self-centered, aimless, or shallow prayer
Prayer is Scripture-informed communion, not vague spirituality or performance

transcript:
## Introduction and Overview

I'm honored to teach you again. Before we begin, I want to offer a couple of things. First, I'm not a master on prayer. I'm barely even a novice. As has been said in this series, prayer is arguably, if not the most difficult spiritual discipline in the Christian life. I want to prejudge myself so that you don't have to—I am not an expert on prayer. This is more convicting for me than any of you. Please take what I share as helpful learning, not as "you should pray like me," because I do not pray like this myself all the time, and I would argue that most of us don't anyway.

Second, there's a lot to get through today. It's going to be very fast—not a train wreck, but it is going to be a roller coaster.

This morning we are diving into our study on the Westminster Larger Catechism, dealing with questions 185 and 186. Third, pretty much all of this material comes from J.G. Vos and his commentary on the Westminster Larger Catechism. I can't say "Vos said this" every time, but if it sounds good, most likely it's not me—it's Vos.

We're dealing with two questions today: 185 and 186. They cover what kind of heart a Christian should pray with and what rule guides us in prayer. We're going to walk phrase by phrase through these—how are we to pray, and what rule God has given us.

## Question 185: How Are We to Pray?

Question 185 asks: "How are we to pray?"

> We are to pray with an awful apprehension of the majesty of God, and deep sense of our own unworthiness, necessities, and sins. With penitent, thankful, and enlarged heart, with understanding, faith, sincerity, fervency, love, and perseverance, waiting upon him with humble submission to his will.

This question contains quite a few adjectives and descriptors. I've broken this down phrase by phrase, trying not to combine one thing into another. I have 15 points here for this question.

### Awful Apprehension of the Majesty of God

The first phrase: "with an awful apprehension of the majesty of God."

Awful does not mean terrible or horrible. It means full of awe—having reverential fear. Consider Hebrews 12:28-29:

> Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom which cannot be shaken, let us have grace, by which we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear. For our God is a consuming fire.

Calvin says in his Institutes: "Men will never worship God with sincerity until they properly understand his majesty." 

In America today, the only thing that's focused on is God's love. I'm not saying us, but generally that's all people know about God—his love. The divines, what, 400 years ago, are emphasizing that God is more than just a loving God. He's majestic, he's powerful, he's infinite, he's eternal, he's great. He is loving, but that is just one aspect of God. We need to have an awful apprehension of the majesty of God in our prayers, not just focus on what love can we get from God.

Vos says: "The first rule of true prayer is reverence. An awareness that we are addressing the infinite personal God."

Ecclesiastes 5:1-2 describes the majesty of God:

> Walk prudently when you go to the house of God, and draw near to hear rather than to give the sacrifice of fools. For they do not know that they do evil. Do not be rash with your mouth, and let not your heart utter anything hastily before God. For God is in heaven and you on earth. Therefore, let your words be few.

Putting this phrase together in modern language: We are to pray with a reverential realization of God's absolute infinite greatness and separation from all created beings.

Why? God and man are not equals. Even before the fall, Adam and Eve could not have enjoyed communion with God if God had not taken the initiative in bridging the chasm between creature and creator. How much more so now, after the fall, when being is separated not only by our finitude but more so by our sinfulness.

### Deep Sense of Our Own Unworthiness

Next clause: "a deep sense of our own unworthiness."

Right off the bat, this is not self-hatred or self-pity. This is humility.

When God is talking to Abraham about destroying Sodom and Gomorrah, they go through their whole exchange: "What if there are 50 righteous men in Sodom?" The Lord says okay, He'll spare it for 50. "What about 45? What about 30? What about 25? What about 10?" But when Abraham is talking to God, Genesis 18:27, he has a sense of his own unworthiness in being able to talk to God:

> Then Abraham answered and said, "Indeed now I who am but dust and ashes have taken it upon myself to speak to the Lord."

That is us. In our prayer, we are dust and ashes. This should keep us from being puffed up when we are talking to God.

John Owen writes: "He who would pray rightly must bring a broken will and a sense of creature poverty."

When you realize who God is, naturally you realize who you are not. Remember: we have no claims on God's love and mercy. Through no power of our own are we able to pray to the Almighty Creator of the universe.

### Deep Sense of Our Necessities

We have a deep sense of our necessities. This is an honest consciousness of our condition—not only our condition physically but spiritually.

A good example is the tax collector and the Pharisee in Luke 18:9-14:

> Also He spoke this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others: "Two men went up to the temple to pray; one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, 'God, I thank You that I am not like other men—extortioners, unjust, adulterers—or even as this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess.' And the tax collector, standing afar off, would not so much as raise his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, 'God, be merciful to me a sinner!' I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted."

The Pharisee does not pray for himself at all. It is just public boasting about all the things he is very good at. He has no sense of his necessities in the eyes of God. Whereas the tax collector has a deep sense that his greatest necessity is for the mercy of God, and that should affect our prayers.

Not just physically but spiritually—there's not like one is better than the other. You can pray for things that you need in this life. That's not unpious or less pious than praying for your heart as well, because God cares for you in all aspects.

### Confession of Sin

We have a deep sense of our own sins. We cannot pray rightly without confessing sin. We can never approach God aright in prayer unless we are willing to acknowledge the truth about ourselves.

First John 1:9 says:

> If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

Thomas Watson, when writing about this, says: "The plaster of Christ's blood is never applied till the wound of sin is open."

In modern medicine, we don't use plaster to heal wounds. But the idea is: if you are not willing to admit you have a wound, you will not take medical care. If a kid who falls off his bike and scrapes his knee says, "I'm fine, I'm fine, I'm fine," he won't accept a bandage.

That should be our attitude in prayer. If we're not willing to admit our sin, we will not receive the grace of forgiveness, repentance, and growth that comes from showing ourselves and God our own sin. He knows our sin, but He's not going to pardon all sin just because we're sinful. You have to confess and admit your own sins in prayer.

### Penitent Heart

Next, we pray with penitent hearts. Repentance is not merely confessing sin but hating it and turning from it.

Why? Vos says: "We must pray with penitent hearts because God's mercy is promised to those who not only confess their sins but sincerely desire to forsake them."

What does a penitent heart look like? Joel 2 speaks of the coming of the day of the Lord. The first 11 verses show what will happen on that day to the people of Israel. In verse 12, asking for repentance, the Lord says:

> "Now therefore," says the Lord, "Turn to Me with all your heart, With fasting, with weeping, and with mourning. So rend your heart, and not your garments; Return to the Lord your God, For He is gracious and merciful, Slow to anger, and of great kindness; And He relents from doing harm."

"Rend your heart and not your garments." This is not an outward penance as we see in some other traditions to pay for our own sins. This is looking at your heart with a microscope—not to bring yourself to despair, but to have an honest realization of what your heart is.

There's a different tradition where you can pay for your own sins by doing different things. You know what I'm talking about—the Roman Catholic Church. When you go to confess and the priest says, "Okay, do this many prayers, walk up the stairs on your knees," that is not a penitent heart. That's outward absurdity. You cannot pay for your own sins that you yourself cannot pay for, and if you are not willing to admit that, you will not be forgiven.

### Thankful Heart

We have penitent hearts, and we have thankful hearts. Thanksgiving should saturate our prayer.

First Thessalonians 5:16-18 says:

> Rejoice always, pray without ceasing; in everything give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.

Colossians 4:2 says:

> Continue earnestly in prayer, being vigilant in it with thanksgiving.

Philippians 4:6 says:

> Be anxious for nothing; but in everything by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.

Not everyone—but most of us, or some of us, or maybe just me—starts every prayer like this: "Dear Lord, thank you for this day," and then the prayer starts, and often that is the beginning and the end of our thanksgiving in prayer.

When people say "count your blessings," I know it's a cliché, but if you actually count your blessings in prayer and are thankful for them, you will realize that you could pray forever and not run out of blessings to count. That is the kind of heart we should have in prayer. It's more than just "Dear Lord, thank you for this day" and then our prayer starts.

Be specific. Be thankful for this, this, this, this, this. It's different for everyone, but God knows you're thankful—yes. But He also commands us to pray with thanksgiving. So be specific in your thankfulness.

### Enlarged Heart

We have a penitent heart, we have a thankful heart, and we have an enlarged heart. What does an enlarged heart look like? It is a heart with a deep desire to receive God's blessings and experience communion with Him. It is a pouring out of your soul, knowing that God can answer your prayer and desiring Him to answer it.

I see this in the prayers of Hannah in 1 Samuel. She was not able to have a child. She was the other wife of Elkanah, who was kind of a dummy. In her sadness and sorrow, he goes to her and says, "Am I not greater to you than 10 sons?" That's an idiot move. But they're out of the feast and everyone's having a good time, but Hannah is in the corner sorrowful. She's praying in her heart, her mouth is moving as we do often. Eli the priest looks over at her and says, "This lady is drunk. She's having a conversation with herself. There's no one around her. She's had too much to drink. It's time to cut her off."

But in 1 Samuel 1:15, Hannah answers:

> "No, my lord, I am a woman of sorrowful spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor intoxicating drink, but have poured out my soul before the Lord."

That is an enlarged heart. In her prayer, she is pouring out her heart to the Lord with a desire for Him to answer her requests. Yes, there is comfort in pouring your heart to the Lord in praying, but she is not praying thinking that the Lord cannot answer her prayer. She is praying with her whole heart, pouring her soul out in faith that He will answer.

No is an answer, and she's willing to accept that. Just because the answer is not yes does not mean the Lord does not answer your prayer.

When her prayers are answered in the way she asks, in 1 Samuel 2:1, she rejoices:

> "My heart rejoices in the Lord; My horn is exalted in the Lord. I smile at my enemies, Because I rejoice in my salvation."

So it is a heart that desires to receive God's blessings and it is pouring out of our soul to Him.

### Understanding

Next, we are to pray with understanding. We pray with our minds, and furthermore, we are to have insight on God's revelation. We need to know the Bible.

In 1 Corinthians 14, Paul is dealing with the Corinthian church about the gifts of the Spirit, particularly speaking in tongues. In 1 Corinthians 14:15, Paul concludes:

> "What is the conclusion then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will also pray with understanding. I will sing with the spirit, and I will also sing with understanding."

Your prayers have to be understandable to you and to those who are hearing them.

The Confession, in chapter 21, paragraph 3, says:

> "Prayer, which is one special part of religious worship, is by God required of all men; and, that it may be accepted, it is to be made in the name of the Son, by the help of the Spirit, according to His will, with understanding, reverence, humility, fervency, faith, love, and perseverance; and, if vocal, in a known tongue."

If it's not a language you understand, don't pray in it. Ignorant prayer is not pious. It is careless. Know what you are asking for. Pray Scripture and pray thoughtfully.

### Faith

Next, we pray with faith. Faith is essential. This is arguably the most important attribute of Christian prayer. To pray without faith is not to pray at all. Prayer without trust is only words spoken into the air. But to pray with faith is to rest our hearts in the reality of who God is—the Creator of heaven and earth, the One who hears the cries of His people, the Father who sent His Son to bear the punishment of our own sin, and the God who cares for us deeply and desires to give what is good according to His will.

Faith takes prayer out of the realm of wishful thinking and anchors it in the character, promises, and redeeming work of God.

Hebrews 11:6 says:

> "But without faith it is impossible to please Him, for he who comes to God must believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him."

You must believe that God exists, and that He is a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him.

Calvin again in his Institutes says: "Prayer flows from faith." You cannot pray unless you have faith. But faith is strengthened by prayer. So faithful prayer flows from faith, and prayer faithfully increases faith. It's circular reasoning, but in a good way.

### Sincerity

We are to pray with sincerity. This means no pretense, no performance.

Matthew 6 lays this out clearly. In all matters of life, at the beginning of Matthew 6, closer to the end of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus contrasts what the Pharisees do with what you should do. This is applicable to every aspect of life:

> Don't practice your righteousness to be seen by others. Don't give with attention or announcement. Don't pray publicly in order to showcase holiness. Don't fast with a gloomy, attention-seeking appearance. Don't seek human praise as a reward for your spiritual actions.

These are all things that do not describe sincerity. Instead:

> Do give in secret, only for God to see. Do pray in private, trusting the Father who hears in secret. Do fast quietly. Do seek to be normal to others. Do seek God's approval, not man's applause. Trust that God rewards what is done in secret.

This is all aspects of life, and it is a good reminder of how to be sincere and what sincerity looks like in our prayers and in all of life.

John Owen, in the Puritan tradition, warns us: "God is not moved by the noise of the words but by the heart."

The application here is: bring your real heart to God, not the polished one.

### Fervency

We pray with sincerity and we pray with fervency. This means earnestness and warmth. This does not mean emotional display, intensity of volume, or dramatic expression.

You can picture a prayer where you have seen that done—maybe in a church that has a lot more people or dimmer lights or many more musical instruments. I'm not saying musical instruments are wrong, but a prayer is not a performance, and that takes away from the fervency of the prayer.

Fervency is a matter of the heart—sincere, earnest, and engaged. It is a right response to who God is and what we are asking of Him. It is a genuine outpouring of the soul to God.

If praying with fervency is a fruit, it takes time to grow. Not everyone is going to be instantly ready for a sincere, warm, earnest prayer, but it must be nurtured. It is not coldness. It is not indifference. It is not mechanical repetition.

As we saw earlier, in praying faithfully, praying with fervency is to pray as though God is real, His promises are true, His glory matters, and His answers truly change things. Without fervency, prayer is motion. With it, prayer is worship.

### Love

Praying with love guards against empty duty. The Pharisees' lack of love made the commandments of God of no effect by their tradition.

In Matthew 15:8, Jesus quoting Isaiah says:

> "These people draw near to Me with their mouth, And honor Me with their lips, But their heart is far from Me."

We have to, but we also get to—because of what God has done for us. We should desire love to talk with Him. Not only that, but because we love one another, we pray for each other.

How often do you find yourself just praying for yourself over and over again, realizing there are other people to pray for? I know that might not be everyone, but that is me often times.

Praying with love leads you to pray for more than just yourself. James 5:16 says:

> "Confess your trespasses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The effective, fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much."

Let me ask you this: which is easier—to do something because you have to, or because you want to? Obviously, a person filled with love turns the "have-tos" into the "want-tos."

If you love your neighbor, if you truly love them, you will want to pray for them. If you truly love your brothers and sisters in Christ, you will want to pray for them. Maybe the hardest and most difficult—if you truly love God, you will want to pray for your enemies.

### Perseverance

We pray with fervency, love, and perseverance. What does it mean to pray with perseverance? Keep praying even when nothing happens.

I can't help but think of faithful mothers and wives praying morning and evening for their wayward son or their rebellious daughter for years and years, never failing to trust that their prayers are heard, even when no evident change is apparent.

Many generations have been kept out of the gates of hell from the prayers of faithful mothers. We can learn something from that, especially us men. I don't know why it is, but women seem to be much better at praying than men. Maybe that is a false observation, but it seems generally true.

This is not just for mothers praying for their children. This is for the whole church. Luke 18:1 says:

> "Then He spoke a parable to them, that men always ought to pray and not lose heart."

That's for all of us.

### Waiting Upon the Lord

We pray with perseverance, waiting upon Him. What does this mean? Waiting is active trust—not passivity. God's will is greater than our will, and His ways are better than ours.

Psalm 27:14 says:

> "Wait on the Lord; Be of good courage, And He shall strengthen your heart; Wait, I say, on the Lord."

Waiting upon the Lord means remaining steadfast when answers are delayed. Waiting upon the Lord is an attitude of confidence not in ourselves but in Him. It is admitting that we are not in control and trusting that what He says in His word is true. This requires humility, of course. It requires hope.

Isaiah 40:31 says:

> "But those who wait on the Lord Shall renew their strength; They shall mount up with wings like eagles, They shall run and not be weary, They shall walk and not faint."

Waiting upon the Lord not only has humility and hope but it protects us from despair and anxiety.

How so? When we change our attitude to an attitude of humbly waiting upon the Lord, then our hope is not in the outcome but in the Lord. The outcome of our prayer is far off, unattainable, and uncertain. But what is here, attainable and certain? The promises of the Lord. Yes, and amen. We have them.

So waiting upon the Lord is praying about our trials and concerns and trusting in His promises, that they are true.

How does it protect us from anxiety? Psalm 94:19 says:

> "In the multitude of my anxieties within me, Your comforts delight my soul."

Here's really the clincher: we are able to hand back our cares, our concerns, our fears to the One who already holds us and the solution. And to the One who loves us more than we can understand.

First Peter 5:7 says:

> "Cast all your cares on Him, because He cares for you."

But we have to let go of them. We can't hand our cares to God and then just try to pull them back so we can stay in control. We have to give them to God and let go. That does not mean let go and then sit there and do nothing. It means give it to God and get going.

### Humble Submission to God's Will

And finally, we pray with humble submission to His will. Our prayers end where Jesus ended: "Not my will, but Yours be done."

In the garden before His crucifixion, Matthew 26:39 says:

> "He went a little farther and fell on His face, and prayed, saying, 'O My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will.'"

The Man facing the worst thing that has ever happened in history—a real thing, I would not like to do this, but if it's going to happen, it is Your will, Lord, and not mine. It should be much easier for us to pray that same thing, knowing that we are never going to face what Jesus has faced. We should be able to yield our desires to God's authority.

We embrace God's no. We embrace the not yet. We embrace the wait, believing with certainty that His answer is better than ours.

Second Corinthians 12:8-9 gives us Paul's example with the thorn in the flesh:

> "Concerning this thing I pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from me. And He said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, my strength is made perfect in weakness.' Therefore most gladly I will rather boast in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me."

Hold your request with open hands. God's way is always better.

With Calvin, we can truly say: "I offer my heart to You, O Lord, promptly and sincerely."

## Questions on Question 185

Do we have questions on the question? No questions? Okay.

Now you may be thinking to yourself, "We've got another question." I'm just going to touch it because we're going to have two lessons on the Lord's Prayer here soon, so I don't want to steal from Nick Anderson or from Mr. Steve Thomas.

## Question 186: What Rule Have God Given for Our Direction in Prayer?

> What rule have God given us for our direction in the duty of prayer? The whole word of God is ordained to direct us in the duty of prayer; but the special rule of direction is that form of prayer which our Savior Christ taught His disciples, commonly called the Lord's Prayer.

### The Whole Word of God Directs Prayer

The first clause: "the whole word of God is ordained to direct us in the duty of prayer."

What is the main idea here? The whole Bible shapes everything about prayer—not just that we pray, but why, how, and for what.

The Holy Scripture commands us to pray. It gives promises that encourage prayer. Scripture records examples that model prayer. And Scripture sets boundaries that keep prayer God-centered.

We saw this already with Hannah's prayer, with David's Psalms, with Solomon dedicating the temple, and with the prayers of the church in Acts.

The whole word of God directs our prayer. What does that mean for us? We are not inventing prayer. We are responding to God's revelation. Prayer is not vaguely spiritual. It is Scripture-informed communion.

### The Special Rule: The Lord's Prayer

"But the special rule of direction is that form of prayer which our Savior Christ taught His disciples, commonly called the Lord's Prayer."

If there is a special rule, then there are other rules that are less special—broader rules. There is the general rule: all of Scripture. And the special rule: the Lord's Prayer, which is contained in all of Scripture but is more direct and more specific.

The Catechism distinguishes here between a general rule—all of Scripture—and the special rule: the Lord's Prayer.

Why is the Lord's Prayer a special rule? 

- It is the only prayer Jesus explicitly taught His disciples.
- It summarizes every category of biblical prayer.
- It guards against self-centered, aimless, or shallow prayer.

This does not mean the Lord's Prayer is the only prayer we may pray. I think we know that. It does mean that the Lord's Prayer is a pattern and it is a measure of praying.

I'm sure Nick Anderson and Mr. Steve Thomas will make everything much clearer. I'm going to move on.

### Jesus Teaching His Disciples to Pray

The form of prayer which our Savior Christ taught His disciples—Jesus did not only teach that we should pray, but how we should pray. We have two accounts of this: Matthew 6 and Luke 11.

In Luke 11, the disciples specifically request: "Teach us to pray." So Jesus, in teaching them to pray, is trying to teach them not to pray as performance.

I think the Lord's Prayer has become one of the most performative prayers maybe in our day.
